title: Getting Started on ARCC MedicineBow
text:
Preface
A practical guide to getting work done on MedicineBow, the University of Wyoming’s high-performance computing (HPC) cluster, run by the Advanced Research Computing Center (ARCC).
It is written for people joining the ASCEND engine and its ARID program, and assumes you are comfortable on a computer but have never used a shared supercomputer. Each chapter explains why before how.

title: Getting Started on ARCC MedicineBow
text:
Why this book exists
The official documentation — the ARCC wiki — is good but has gaps and is in places out of date. The content here was written while onboarding on the live cluster and cross-checked against the running system in July 2026. Where the docs and the machine disagree, this book follows the machine and notes the conflict.






This is not an official ARCC document



It’s a community onboarding guide. It can drift out of date, and ARCC can change policy at any time. When in doubt, the official wiki and arcc-help@uwyo.edu are authoritative. Corrections are very welcome.

title: Getting Started on ARCC MedicineBow
text:
Quick orientation

Request your account by emailing Virginia Iglesias (virginia@innosphere.org), who coordinates ASCEND/ARID access. (See Getting an account.)
Nothing on the cluster is backed up. Not home, not project, not scratch. There are snapshots, but they live on the same array. (See Where your data lives.)
Never run real computation on a login node. Log in, then hand work to the scheduler (Slurm) or grab an interactive session. (See Why a scheduler exists.)
Every job must name your project account with --account=<project>. (See Anatomy of a batch job.)
The partition and QOS you choose decide how long you wait and how big you can go. Short test runs and long simulations belong in different queues (Partitions and QOS on MedicineBow, Queue times: which partition for what).

title: Getting Started on ARCC MedicineBow
text:
How the book is organized
The chapters run in the order you’ll need them:

Getting started on the cluster — what an HPC cluster is, how to request an account, and first login through the portal and SSH keys.
Linux essentials — the minimum shell you need: moving around, editing files, and keeping work alive across a dropped connection with tmux.
Storage and moving data — the three filesystems (and the fact that nothing is backed up), plus Globus, rsync, and rclone for transfers.
Software: modules, conda, and containers — loading software with Lmod, using conda without filling your home directory, and running containers with Apptainer.
Running jobs with Slurm — why a scheduler exists, the anatomy of a batch job, and asking for the right resources.
Partitions, QOS, and queue times — which hardware and service tier to choose, measured wait times, and how job priority is actually computed here.
Monitoring, arrays, and interactive jobs — watching and diagnosing jobs, job arrays, interactive and GPU sessions, and the parallelism ladder.
Preemption, checkpointing, and failures — surviving the condo model and walltime limits, and reading the wreckage when a job fails.
Reference — a command cheat sheet, a symptom-to-fix troubleshooting index, and a glossary.

title: 1  Getting started on the cluster
text:
1.1.1 Mental model
MedicineBow is not one big computer. It is a few hundred ordinary Linux servers (“nodes”) wired together, all mounting the same shared filesystems, all managed by a program that decides whose job runs where and when. That program is the scheduler (here, Slurm). Learning the cluster is mostly learning to work with the scheduler.


1.1.2 Login nodes vs. compute nodes
There are two kinds of machines, and confusing them is the most common beginner mistake.
Login nodes (mblog1, mblog2) are the front door. When you ssh in or open a terminal in the web portal, you land here. They are shared by everyone at once — dozens of people editing files, submitting jobs, and moving data. Use them for lightweight work: editing scripts, managing files, compiling small things, submitting and checking jobs.
Compute nodes are where computation happens. You never SSH to them directly; you ask the scheduler for one (or many), and it gives you exclusive, accounted-for access for a bounded time. The default mb nodes have 96 CPU cores and ~1 TB of RAM each, and the GPU nodes carry up to 8 NVIDIA H100s.






flowchart LR
    U["Your laptop"] -->|"ssh / web portal"| L
    subgraph MB ["MedicineBow"]
        L["Login nodes<br/>mblog1 / mblog2<br/>shared, lightweight only"]
        S{{"Slurm scheduler"}}
        L -->|"sbatch / salloc"| S
        S --> C1["Compute node"]
        S --> C2["Compute node"]
        S --> C3["GPU node"]
    end
    FS[("Shared filesystems<br/>home, project, scratch")]
    L --- FS
    C1 --- FS
    C3 --- FS
    style MB fill:#f3eefb,stroke:#7a4fb5,color:#3a2a5a




Figure 1.1: You reach a shared login node from your laptop; the scheduler runs your jobs on dedicated compute nodes. All nodes see the same filesystems.











Don’t compute on login nodes



A heavy job on mblog1/mblog2 — a big simulation, a data-crunching Python script, a multi-hour build — slows the machine for everyone logging in. ARCC monitors this and kills runaway login-node processes (and emails you).
Rule of thumb: anything that takes more than a couple of minutes, or uses more than a core or two, belongs in a Slurm job or an interactive session. See Section 5.1.




1.1.3 Why share a machine at all?
If everyone had their own dedicated server, most servers would sit idle while a few people occasionally needed far more than one server could give. Pooling the hardware and scheduling access means:

When you need 50 nodes for an ensemble, you can have them (briefly).
When you need nothing, someone else uses the hardware you’re not using.
A fair-share accounting system stops any one person from hogging everything.

In exchange, you sometimes wait in line and you have to describe your work up front (how many cores, how much memory, how long). Most of this book is about making those two things painless.


1.1.4 What MedicineBow is, concretely
MedicineBow is a RHEL 9 Linux cluster. Its hardware is a mix of:

General CPU nodes (the mb partition): 25 nodes, 96 cores and ~1 TB RAM each.
GPU nodes: H100, L40S, A30, A6000, and R6000 flavors — for ML, PINNs, and anything CUDA.
Absorbed older clusters: the retired Teton, Beartooth, and WildIris clusters now live on as large partitions inside MedicineBow. Teton alone is ~250 nodes.
Investor (“condo”) nodes: hardware bought by specific research groups, which others can borrow when it’s idle — but the owner can reclaim it and bump your job (see Section 8.1).

The partition chapter (Section 6.1) covers which hardware to ask for, and the queue-times chapter (Section 6.2) covers which choices leave you waiting versus running now.

Channel

Anything. Real humans, ticketed via Jira Service Management.

Tuesdays, 11am–1pm — bring your actual problem.

1.2 Getting an account

1.2.1 How to request an account
Access to MedicineBow for ASCEND/ARID performers is coordinated through the program. To request an account, email Virginia Iglesias (virginia@innosphere.org) and mention that you’re an ASCEND/ARID performer who needs MedicineBow access. She’ll arrange for you to be added to the project.
Accounts are tied to a project — for this work that’s cowy-firesurro (the project this guide was written under), which is also the name you type into every job you run (Section 5.2).


1.2.2 UW accounts vs. ARCC-Only accounts
ASCEND spans UW, CSU, CU Boulder, Mines, NCAR, and NEON, so this distinction affects collaborators:

ARCC-Only accounts and Globus



External collaborators on ARCC-Only accounts cannot use Globus, the recommended way to move large datasets (Section 3.2). They’ll need a guest collection set up for them, or a UW person to broker transfers. Plan for this early if your data lives at CSU or NCAR.




1.2.3 The free tier
Each researcher’s baseline allocation:

100,000 CPU core-hours per year
20,000 GPU-hours per year

That is plenty for getting started — 100,000 core-hours is roughly one 96-core node running flat out for six weeks. Larger allocations and investor projects exist beyond this. Core-hours are counted as (cores × wall-clock hours), a reason not to over-ask for resources (Section 5.3).


1.2.4 The practical checklist

Email Virginia Iglesias (virginia@innosphere.org) to request a MedicineBow account, mentioning that you’re an ASCEND/ARID performer.
You’ll be added to the project and issued a UW username. Your first login is



If you’re an external (non-UW) collaborator, say so — you’ll get an ARCC-Only account, which can’t use Globus (Section 3.2), so ask how you’ll move data.

No VPN is required to reach ARCC, on campus or off, so once your account exists you can log in from anywhere.

section: 1.3 First login, the portal, and SSH keys
text:
1.3 First login, the portal, and SSH keys

1.3.1 Two ways in: portal and SSH
MedicineBow has a single hostname that serves both the web portal and SSH: medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu.

The web portal (Open OnDemand) is a browser interface: a file explorer, a terminal, job submission forms, and interactive apps (desktop sessions, RStudio, Jupyter). Start here on day one.
SSH is the terminal way in, and how you’ll work day-to-day once set up. It requires a key you generate through the portal first.







Don’t use “Southpass”



Older notes may point you at southpass.arcc.uwyo.edu, the portal for the retired Beartooth cluster. The DNS name still resolves but has no live service behind it. The current portal is medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu.




1.3.2 Step 1 — Log into the portal
Go to https://medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu and sign in with your UW username and password. You’ll be prompted for Duo two-factor authentication. If you’ve never set up Duo, do it at https://wyosecure.uwyo.edu. No VPN is needed.
Once in, note the Files menu (browse /home, /project, /gscratch), the Clusters → Shell option (a terminal in your browser), and the Interactive Apps menu.


1.3.3 Step 2 — Generate your SSH key with the SSH Key Manager
SSH on MedicineBow is key-and-certificate based, not password based. Generate a key pair through the portal:

In the portal, open the SSH Key Manager.
Generate a key. It downloads as a zip named after your username.
Unpack it into your local ~/.ssh and fix permissions:

unzip ~/Downloads/<username>.zip -d ~/.ssh
chmod 0600 -R ~/.ssh
ssh-add
Now you can connect from your own terminal:
ssh <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu






SSH keys expire after one year



Roughly a year after setup, your ssh stops working — permission denied, no obvious reason. The key expired. Go back to the portal’s SSH Key Manager, generate a fresh key, and unzip it into ~/.ssh again. This is by design.




1.3.4 Step 3 — A comfortable SSH config (optional)
Add this to ~/.ssh/config on your laptop so you can just type ssh medbow:
Host medbow
    HostName medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu
    User <username>
    ServerAliveInterval 60
    ServerAliveCountMax 5
ServerAliveInterval sends a small keepalive every 60 seconds so campus/VPN firewalls don’t silently drop your connection while you’re reading output.


1.3.5 Which door should I use?







You want to…
Use




First-time setup, generate SSH keys
Portal (required)


A quick browser terminal from any machine
Portal → Clusters → Shell


A graphical desktop, RStudio, Jupyter
Portal → Interactive Apps


Everyday scripting, editing, job submission
SSH from your terminal


Drag-and-drop a few files
Portal → Files (for big data, see Section 3.2)



Once you can log in and get a shell prompt, continue to the Linux survival kit (Chapter 2), or skip ahead to storage (Section 3.1) and Slurm (Section 5.1) if you already know a terminal.

title: 2  Linux essentials
text:
2.1 Moving around
If you already live in a terminal, skim the tmux section. Everything here is standard Linux; nothing is ARCC-specific except the paths.
Three shortcuts you’ll use constantly: ~ is your home directory, . is “here”, and .. is “up one”. Press Tab to complete a half-typed path.

title: 2  Linux essentials
text:
pwd                 # where am I?
ls -lh              # list files, human-readable sizes
cd /project/cowy-firesurro   # go somewhere
cd                  # go home ($HOME)
cd -                # go back to where you just were

title: 2  Linux essentials
section: 2.2 Looking at files without opening them
text:
2.2 Looking at files without opening them
cat file.txt          # dump a whole (small) file
less big.log          # page through a big file; q to quit, / to search
head -n 20 file       # first 20 lines
tail -n 50 file       # last 50 lines
tail -f slurm-123.out # follow a job's output live as it's written
tail -f on a job’s output file shows whether it’s doing anything.

title: 2  Linux essentials
text:
2.3 Editing files
nano is the easy choice — arrow keys work, and shortcuts are listed at the bottom of the screen (^O = save, ^X = exit).
nano submit.sh
vim is powerful but has a learning curve; if you don’t know it, nano is fine for a submit script. For anything bigger, edit on your laptop and use the portal’s file browser, VS Code’s Remote-SSH, or rsync (Section 3.2).

title: 2  Linux essentials
text:
2.4 Finding things
grep -r "account" .          # search file contents recursively
find . -name "*.nc"          # find files by name
find . -size +1G             # find files bigger than 1 GB (great for quota hunts)
du -sh *                     # how big is each thing in this directory?
du -sh * | sort -h finds what’s eating your quota — useful given the 50 GB home limit (Section 3.1).

title: 2  Linux essentials
text:
2.5 Environment variables and your shell
Your shell remembers settings in variables. A few you’ll meet:
echo $HOME        # /home/<username>
echo $USER        # your username
echo $SCRATCH     # /gscratch/<username> — your scratch space
echo $PATH        # where the shell looks for commands
To make something permanent (say, a handy alias), add it to ~/.bashrc:
alias q='squeue --me'          # see just my jobs
alias proj='cd /project/cowy-firesurro'
Run source ~/.bashrc (or log out and back in) to apply changes.

title: 2  Linux essentials
section: 2.6 tmux: keep work alive across a dropped connection
text:
2.6 tmux: keep work alive across a dropped connection
When you SSH in and start something, closing your laptop or losing WiFi kills that shell and everything running in it. tmux keeps your session alive on the login node whether or not you’re connected.
tmux new -s work     # start a named session "work"
#   ... do things, launch an interactive job, watch output ...
#   detach with:  Ctrl-b then d
tmux ls              # list your sessions
tmux attach -t work  # reattach later, even from a different computer
The workflow:

SSH into the login node.
tmux new -s work.
Inside tmux, do your editing, submit jobs, launch an interactive session (Section 7.3).
Detach (Ctrl-b then d) and close your laptop. It all keeps running.
Tomorrow, SSH back in and tmux attach -t work — exactly where you left off.







tmux is for login-node shells, not batch jobs



A batch job (sbatch, Section 5.2) already runs independently of your connection — log out and it keeps going. tmux is for things that live in your shell: interactive sessions, monitoring, an editor you don’t want to lose.

title: 2  Linux essentials
text:
2.7 Permissions, briefly
You’ll occasionally see chmod and permission strings like -rw-r-----. The main uses are fixing your SSH keys (chmod 0600 -R ~/.ssh, from Section 1.3) and making a script executable:
chmod +x run.sh
There is no sudo on the cluster. You can’t install system packages or change things outside your own directories, and you don’t need to — everything you install goes in your own space (Section 4.2) or as modules (Section 4.1).

title: 3  Storage and moving data
text:
3.1 Where your data lives
The three filesystems, what each one promises, and how to get data in and out.

title: 3  Storage and moving data
text:
3.1.1 Nothing is backed up
Nothing on MedicineBow is backed up. Not home, not project, not scratch.
There are snapshots (point-in-time copies you can sometimes restore from), but they live on the same storage array as your live data — if the array fails, the snapshots fail with it. Snapshots protect against accidental deletion, not hardware loss. Anything you can’t afford to lose needs a copy elsewhere: your institution’s storage, a cloud bucket, or the separate Alcova service, which does have real nightly backups.

Check your usage and limits for home, scratch, and project:
arccquota

3.1.2.1 /home — small, personal, for config not data
50 GB fills fast once a conda environment eats 15 GB of it. Home is for dotfiles, scripts, and small configs — not datasets and not software installs. When home fills up, things break (jobs fail to write logs, logins misbehave), so watch it with arccquota and du -sh ~/* | sort -h.


3.1.2.2 /project/<proj> — the shared workhorse
5 TB, shared by everyone on your project (e.g. cowy-firesurro). This is where shared datasets, inputs, and results belong. Agree on a directory convention with your group so you don’t clobber each other. It persists for 6 months after the project ends.


3.1.2.3 /gscratch/$USER — fast and disposable
Also 5 TB, and the fast filesystem — use it as the working directory for jobs with heavy I/O. Files untouched for 90 days are purged automatically. Never keep the only copy of anything here.






Scratch purge is 90 days, not 45



Legacy Confluence docs say 45 days; the current ARCC wiki says 90. Both pages are live, but 90 is the current policy. Either way, don’t treat scratch as storage.




3.1.2.4 /lscratch — node-local, gone when the job ends
Each compute node has its own local disk at /lscratch. It’s the fastest storage available to a job (no network in the way), ideal for scratch files a single job reads and rewrites constantly. It’s wiped when your job ends, so copy anything you want to keep back to /project or /gscratch before the job exits.
(There is no /data filesystem, despite what some docs suggest.)



3.1.3 Install software in project space, not home






Install software into /project/<proj>/software, not /home



Your project has an extra 250 GB quota at /project/<proj>/software for installing software. A single conda environment with a few scientific packages can be 10–20 GB — two of those fills a 50 GB home directory.
Point conda, pip, R libraries, and manual builds at project software space from the start. The conda chapter (Section 4.2) shows how.




3.1.4 A sane layout to adopt on day one
/home/<you>/                      # dotfiles, small scripts, SSH keys
/project/cowy-firesurro/
    software/                     # conda envs, container images, manual builds
    data/                         # shared input datasets
    <you>/                        # your working area within the project
/gscratch/<you>/                  # active job working dirs, heavy I/O, big temp output

title: 3  Storage and moving data
text:
3.2 Moving data in and out

3.2.1 Pick the right tool for the size of the job



Transfer
Best tool




Hundreds of GB / TB, or must-not-corrupt datasets
Globus


A few files, a script, a config
scp or rsync over SSH


To/from cloud storage (S3, Google Drive, etc.)
rclone


Drag-and-drop a handful of files in a browser
Portal → Files



There is no dedicated data-transfer node (DTN) — CLI transfers go through the login nodes, and Globus manages its own endpoint. Another reason to prefer Globus for big moves: it won’t tie up (or get killed on) a shared login node.


3.2.2 Globus — the recommended path for real data
Globus transfers between “collections” (endpoints). It’s restartable, checksums what it moves, retries failures, and runs server-side, so you can start a multi-hundred-GB transfer, close your laptop, and get an email when it’s done.

Log in at https://app.globus.org (choose “University of Wyoming” as your organization, or your own institution).
Search collections for uwyo-ARCC and pick “Medicine Bow”.
The Medicine Bow collection’s root is cluster, so your project shows up at a path like /cluster/medbow/project/cowy-firesurro/....
Set the other side to your institutional or personal collection (install Globus Connect Personal on your own machine to make it an endpoint), pick files, and hit Start.







Globus needs a full UW account



ARCC-Only accounts (external collaborators — Section 1.2) cannot use Globus. If your data lives at CSU, CU, or NCAR and you’re on an ARCC-Only account, you’ll need a UW-side person to broker the transfer, or a guest collection set up for you.




3.2.3 scp and rsync — fine for small, everyday transfers
From your laptop, push a file up:
scp results.csv <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu:/project/cowy-firesurro/<you>/
Pull one down:
scp <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu:/gscratch/<you>/output.nc .
rsync is better for directories and for resuming — it only copies what changed, so an interrupted transfer picks up where it left off:
rsync -avP ./localdir/ <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu:/project/cowy-firesurro/<you>/dir/
The -P flag shows progress and enables resume; -a preserves timestamps and permissions. For more than a few GB, prefer Globus — a login-node scp of a huge file competes with everyone else’s login-node activity and will be slow.


3.2.4 rclone — cloud storage (S3, Google Drive, Box…)
rclone is ARCC’s recommended CLI for moving data to and from cloud services. It’s a module:
module load rclone/1.63.1
rclone config          # one-time: set up a "remote" (S3 bucket, Drive, etc.)
rclone copy mydata/ myremote:bucket/path/    # copy up
rclone copy myremote:bucket/path/ ./mydata/  # copy down
rclone verifies and retries, and handles many small files far better than a loop of scps.


3.2.5 A quick decision guide

Moving your project’s primary dataset onto the cluster? Globus.
Iterating on a submit script from your laptop? rsync (or edit in the portal).
Pulling results into a cloud bucket for a collaborator? rclone.
External collaborator without Globus? Ask your UW PI about a guest collection.

Next: making software available, starting with the module system (Section 4.1).

title: 4  Software: modules, conda, and containers
text:
4.1 Software modules
How software is provided on the cluster, and how to install your own without filling your home directory.
crumbs: 4  Software: modules, conda, and containers

title: 4  Software: modules, conda, and containers
text:
4.1.1 Why modules exist
A cluster has hundreds of users who need incompatible software: three versions of Python, five compilers, conflicting builds of GDAL. Modules let you load exactly the versions you want into your shell for this session, without affecting anyone else. Load a module and its programs appear on your PATH; unload it and they vanish.
module load gcc/14.2.0        # add gcc 14 to this shell
module list                   # what do I currently have loaded?
module unload gcc/14.2.0      # remove it
module purge                  # clear everything and start clean


4.1.2 The hierarchy
MedicineBow uses Lmod in hierarchical mode. Modules are arranged in layers:

Core modules are always visible: the compilers (gcc, nvhpc-sdk, oneapi), MPI, and standalone tools.
Compiler-dependent modules — Python, R, GDAL, NetCDF, HDF5, CUDA — are hidden until you load a compiler. They were built against a specific compiler, so Lmod won’t show them until you’ve picked one.

So a new user runs module avail, doesn’t see gdal, and concludes it isn’t installed. It is — just one layer down.






Use module spider, not module avail, to check whether something exists



module avail shows only what’s loadable given what you’ve already loaded. module spider searches the entire tree and tells you both that something exists and what to load first to reach it.
module spider gdal            # yes it exists; here are the versions
module spider gdal/3.13.0     # ...and exactly what to load before it


A typical geospatial stack, in order:
module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0        # 1. a compiler, first
module load gdal/3.13.0       # 2. now GDAL is reachable
module load netcdf-c/4.9.2-ompi


4.1.3 What’s installed (a tour)
Ask the machine for the current list with module spider, but roughly:

Compilers (core): gcc/{11.4.0, 11.5.0, 13.2.0, 14.2.0, 15.2.0}, nvhpc-sdk, oneapi, openmpi/5.0.10.
After loading a compiler: python/{3.10.6, 3.12.0, 3.14.4}, r/{4.4.0, 4.5.3}, gdal/{3.7.3, 3.13.0}, netcdf-c/4.9.2-ompi, hdf5/1.14.3*, cuda-toolkit/{12.4.1, 12.6.1}, openmpi/4.1.6, rclone/1.63.1.
Standalone: apptainer/{1.3.5, 1.4.1}, singularity/4.1.0, miniconda3/24.3.0, julia/{1.10.3, 1.11.6}.







CUDA needs the deprecated gcc/13.2.0



gcc/13.2.0 prints a deprecation warning pointing to gcc/14.2.0, but cuda-toolkit is only built against gcc/13.2.0. GPU users have to load it anyway:
module load gcc/13.2.0        # the one that warns you — CUDA needs it
module load cuda-toolkit/12.6.1
Ignore the warning here; it’s a packaging quirk.




4.1.4 Making a set of modules load automatically
Once you know the stack a project needs, save it as a named collection so you don’t retype it:
module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 gdal/3.13.0 netcdf-c/4.9.2-ompi
module save geostack          # remember this set as "geostack"

# next session:
module restore geostack
Prefer module restore in submit scripts over hand-loading a long list — it’s reproducible and self-documents the environment your job needs.






Load modules in your submit script, not just interactively



Modules loaded on the login node don’t carry into a batch job. Put the module load / module restore lines inside your sbatch script so the job builds the same environment every time (Section 5.2).


When a package isn’t available as a module — or you need a pip/conda world — see the next chapter (Section 4.2).

title: 4  Software: modules, conda, and containers
text:
4.2 Conda and containers

4.2.1 Point conda away from home first
The miniconda3 module gives you conda:
module load miniconda3/24.3.0
By default, conda writes environments and a package cache into ~/.conda and ~/miniconda3, inside your 50 GB home quota. A couple of scientific environments will fill it. Before creating any environments, point conda at your project’s 250 GB software space.
Create ~/.condarc:
pkgs_dirs:
  - /project/cowy-firesurro/software/<you>/conda/pkgs
envs_dirs:
  - /project/cowy-firesurro/software/<you>/conda/envs
Now new environments and the download cache land in project space:
conda create -n geo python=3.12 numpy xarray netcdf4
conda activate geo






Set .condarc before your first conda create



Environments created before you set .condarc are stranded in home. If you’ve already made the mess: conda env list, remove the home-based envs, and recreate them under project space.


Other conda notes:

No mamba is installed on the cluster; use conda directly.
Activate conda inside your submit script, not just interactively, so batch jobs get the same environment (Section 5.2).
conda clean -a reclaims space from the package cache.



4.2.2 Apptainer: containers for reproducibility and portability
A container bundles an application with its entire operating-system environment into a single image file. On HPC the runtime is Apptainer (formerly Singularity). It runs containers as you, with no root, which makes it the HPC-safe alternative to Docker.
module load apptainer/1.4.1

# Pull a Docker image and convert it to an Apptainer image (.sif):
apptainer pull mytool.sif docker://ghcr.io/someorg/mytool:latest

# Run something inside it:
apptainer exec mytool.sif mytool --help

# Bind your data into the container so it can see it:
apptainer exec --bind /project/cowy-firesurro:/data mytool.sif mytool /data/input.nc
Store .sif images in /project/<proj>/software — they can be large.

text:
5.1 Why a scheduler exists
The scheduler, the anatomy of a batch job, and how to ask for the right resources.

title: 5  Running jobs with Slurm
text:
5.1.1 Why share a machine
With 300 researchers, 300 nodes, and no scheduler, everyone logs into whatever node looks idle and starts running. Two jobs land on the same node and thrash its memory until both crash. A two-week run occupies the node you need for a five-minute test. Nobody can tell whether a node is free.
Slurm replaces “grab a node and hope” with a contract:

You describe the work: resources and a time limit.
Slurm reserves exactly that, on nodes that can provide it, and accounts for it.
Your job runs with those resources guaranteed and isolated from other jobs.
When your time limit is up, the job ends, which keeps the line moving.



5.1.2 The two ways to run work
Batch jobs (sbatch) are the normal mode: you write a script that lists the resources you need and the commands to run, submit it, and walk away. Slurm runs it when your turn comes and writes the output to a file. Use this for essentially all real computation. (Section 5.2)
Interactive jobs (salloc) give you a live shell on a compute node for debugging, exploring data, or developing a script. You still go through the scheduler and consume your allocation, but you get a prompt instead of a script. (Section 7.3)
Both run on compute nodes, not the login node (Section 1.1).


5.1.3 The three questions every job answers
Whether batch or interactive, you tell Slurm three things:








Question
Directive
Covered in




Who pays? (which project)
--account
Section 5.2


How much, and how long?
--cpus-per-task, --mem, --time, …
Section 5.3


What kind of node, and how urgent?
--partition, --qos
Section 6.1



Get these right and jobs run smoothly. Get them wrong and you wait a long time, get rejected at submit time, or watch the job die partway through. The sections that follow take them one at a time.


5.1.4 A first look at the tools
You’ll meet these properly later; here’s the vocabulary:
sbatch submit.sh        # submit a batch job
salloc ...              # get an interactive session
squeue --me             # what are my jobs doing?
scancel <jobid>         # cancel a job
sacct -j <jobid>        # after the fact: what happened, and how much did it use?
ARCC also ships friendlier wrappers — showjobreasons (“why isn’t my job running?”), showuserlimits (“what am I allowed to ask for?”), showpartitions, sqos — used in Section 6.1 and Section 7.1.

title: 5  Running jobs with Slurm
text:
5.2 Anatomy of a batch job

5.2.1 The smallest useful job
Here is a complete, working submit script. Save it as submit.sh:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=cowy-firesurro     # WHO PAYS — the one you can't omit
#SBATCH --job-name=hello
#SBATCH --time=00:10:00              # 10 minutes; jobs are killed at the limit
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=4G                     # always set memory explicitly (see below)
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out        # %j is replaced by the job ID

echo "Running on host: $(hostname)"
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID started at $(date)"

module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 python/3.12.0

python my_analysis.py

echo "Finished at $(date)"
Submit it:
sbatch submit.sh
# Submitted batch job 123456
Watch it and read the output:
squeue --me                 # is it pending / running?
tail -f slurm-123456.out    # follow output as it's written
That’s the loop: write script, sbatch, watch, read output.


5.2.2 The required directive: --account
#SBATCH --account=cowy-firesurro






--account is your project, not your username



Every job on MedicineBow must specify an account, and it’s the project name (cowy-firesurro), not your login name. Leave it out and the job is rejected immediately. This is the most common first error. Confirm your exact project name when you get your account (Section 1.2) and put it in every script, or set it once as a default:
# add to ~/.bashrc so you never forget it
export SBATCH_ACCOUNT=cowy-firesurro
Even so, keep --account in the script itself. It documents intent and survives being run by a collaborator whose default differs.

#SBATCH lines must come before any real commands; the first non-comment, non-#SBATCH line ends the directive block. After that, it’s a bash script that runs on the compute node.


5.2.4 Set memory explicitly






The 10 GB-per-core default on mb



On the default mb partition, if you don’t set --mem, Slurm gives you 10 GB per CPU core (DefMemPerCPU=10000). So this request:
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8       # and no --mem line
asks for 80 GB of RAM, which is harder to schedule than the 8 GB you probably needed, so the job queues longer. Set --mem (whole-job) or --mem-per-cpu explicitly. Covered in depth in Section 5.3.




5.2.5 Making the environment reproducible
A batch job starts in a mostly clean environment. Build the environment you need inside the script so it runs the same way every time, independent of what you had loaded at submit time:
module purge
module restore geostack        # a saved module set (see @sec-modules)
# or, for conda:
module load miniconda3/24.3.0
conda activate geo


5.2.6 Useful variables inside a job
Slurm sets environment variables your script can use:
$SLURM_JOB_ID          # the job's ID
$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK   # cores you were given — pass to your program's thread count
$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID   # which array element this is (see @sec-arrays)
$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR      # the directory you ran sbatch from
A common pattern matches your program’s threads to what Slurm gave you:
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
The next section covers asking for the right resources (Section 5.3); choosing the right queue comes after (Section 6.1).

title: 5  Running jobs with Slurm
text:
5.3 Asking for resources

5.3.1 Cores, tasks, and the words Slurm uses
For most jobs you need two ideas:

A task is one instance of your program. Most jobs are a single task.
CPUs per task is how many cores that program can use (its threads).

#SBATCH --nodes=1                # keep a job on one node unless it's true MPI
#SBATCH --ntasks=1               # one program instance
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8        # that can use 8 cores

Single-threaded program? --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=1.
Multithreaded (OpenMP, most numpy/xarray work)? --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=N, and set export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK.
MPI across many nodes? Use --nodes and --ntasks, and launch with srun (Section 7.4).

Asking for 8 cores does not make a single-threaded program faster; it reserves 7 idle cores and makes you wait longer. Match the request to what your code can use.


5.3.2 Memory
Set memory explicitly, every time. Two ways:
#SBATCH --mem=32G              # total memory for the whole job (simplest)
# or
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=4G       # memory per core (scales with --cpus-per-task)






The 10 GB/core default on mb



If you omit --mem on the default partition, you get 10 GB per core, so --cpus-per-task=8 becomes an 80 GB request. That queues slower and can be rejected if it exceeds a limit. Set your memory explicitly. (Full story in Section 5.2.)


For a first run, estimate a bit high so the job isn’t killed, then measure and right-size (below). A job that exceeds its memory request is killed by the out-of-memory (OOM) killer (Section 8.2), so memory is the one resource where running out is fatal rather than slow.


5.3.3 Time
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00        # HH:MM:SS  (or D-HH:MM:SS, e.g. 2-00:00:00)
Your job is killed the instant it hits this limit, so the request must exceed the real runtime; pad by roughly 25%. Don’t pad wildly, though: a shorter time limit means a lower QOS ceiling and better odds of backfilling into gaps, so it often starts sooner (Section 6.2).






No per-partition default time, so set --time



Partitions on MedicineBow don’t set a default wall time. Without --time, you inherit the partition maximum (7 days), which your QOS will likely reject (the normal QOS caps at 3 days). Always set --time yourself.




5.3.4 Over-asking slows you down
A bigger request is a rarer set of free resources to find:

More cores / memory → fewer nodes can satisfy you → longer wait, and you’re charged for cores you didn’t use.
More time → lower-priority QOS tier and fewer backfill opportunities → longer wait.
A GPU you don’t use → you sit in the busy GPU queue for nothing (Section 6.2).

The fix is to right-size.


5.3.5 Measure, then right-size, with seff
After a job finishes, seff tells you what it actually used versus what you reserved:
seff 123456
Job ID: 123456
State: COMPLETED
Cores: 8
CPU Efficiency: 24.13% of 04:16:00 core-walltime      <- you used ~2 of 8 cores
Memory Utilized: 5.31 GB
Memory Efficiency: 16.59% of 32.00 GB                 <- 32G reserved, 5G used
Read that as: next time ask for ~2 cores and ~8 GB. Low CPU efficiency means you reserved cores your code can’t use; low memory efficiency means you can ask for far less and start sooner.
Check what you’re allowed to ask for with ARCC’s helper:
showuserlimits
Next: where to send the job — partitions and QOS, and their queue-time consequences (Section 6.1, Section 6.2).

title: 6  Partitions, QOS, and queue times
text:
6.3 How priority is computed

6.3.1 The formula
Slurm computes a priority score for every pending job and runs the highest scores first (subject to backfill, below). The score is a weighted sum; MedicineBow’s weights are:
PriorityWeightQOS       = 200     <- dominant
PriorityWeightFairShare = 100
PriorityWeightJobSize   = 100
PriorityWeightAge       = 10
PriorityWeightPartition = 0       (partition doesn't affect priority here)
Each factor is a number between 0 and 1, multiplied by its weight, and summed. The biggest lever, by a wide margin, is QOS.


6.3.2 What each factor means
QOS (weight 200). Higher-priority QOS means a better position. From Section 6.1: interactive (90) > fast (80) > normal (70) > long (60). Choosing fast over long is worth more priority than any amount of waiting, which is why the short-vs-long decision in Section 6.2 matters.
Fair-share (weight 100) — recent usage. Slurm tracks how much your account has used lately relative to its share. Heavy use this week lowers your fair-share factor, and thus your priority, for a while; it recovers as usage decays (half-life ~7 days here). This mechanism stops any one group from monopolizing the machine and rewards steady use over bursts.
Job size (weight 100). A factor based on the resources requested. With the SMALL_RELATIVE_TO_TIME flag this cluster sets, it interacts with your time request — another reason not to over-ask (Section 5.3).
Age (weight 10) — time spent waiting. A job gains priority the longer it sits, maxing out after ~3 days. At weight 10, age is a tie-breaker, not a strategy; you won’t age past someone who chose a better QOS.


6.3.3 Practical takeaway






QOS dominates priority



Because QOS is weighted 2× fair-share and 20× age, the highest-leverage choice for start time is the most appropriate high-priority QOS your job fits — the shortest walltime tier that still lets it finish (Section 6.2). Waiting longer, resubmitting, or submitting at 3am have little effect by comparison.




6.3.4 Backfill: why a small job can jump the line
Priority sets the order, but Slurm also backfills: if the top job is waiting for, say, 40 nodes to free up, Slurm slots a smaller, shorter job into the gap now, as long as that doesn’t delay the top job’s reserved start time. This is why a 20-minute test can start immediately even when the queue looks deep, and why short jobs start sooner than long ones. Requesting less time and fewer resources makes your job backfill-eligible in more gaps — another payoff for right-sizing.


6.3.5 Seeing your own priority
sprio -j <jobid>            # the priority breakdown for a pending job
sprio -l                    # all pending jobs, with factor columns
showjobreasons <jobid>      # ARCC helper: plain-language "why am I waiting?"
If sprio shows a low QOS factor because you’re on long but the job would finish in 10 hours, resubmitting under fast is the most effective change you can make.

Figure 7.1: A job waits (PENDING), runs, then reaches one terminal state. TIMEOUT and OUT_OF_MEMORY mean you under-requested; preemption sends the job back to PENDING.







7.1.2 After it finishes: did it work, and was it sized right?
sacct -j 123456 --format=JobID,State,Elapsed,MaxRSS,ReqMem,TotalCPU,ExitCode
Key columns: State (COMPLETED, FAILED, TIMEOUT, OUT_OF_MEMORY, CANCELLED), Elapsed (wall time used vs. your --time), MaxRSS (peak memory actually used vs. your --mem), and ExitCode.
seff is a friendlier summary:
seff 123456
It prints CPU and memory efficiency as percentages. Low numbers mean you over-asked — reduce the request next time to start sooner (Section 5.3).


7.1.3 ARCC’s own helpers
These live on your PATH by default and each replaces several squeue/scontrol commands:
showuserjobs                # everything you (and optionally others) have queued/running
showjob 123456              # a rich, readable view of one job
shownode mbcpu-001          # what's running on a given node, and how loaded it is
showuserlimits              # what am I actually allowed to request?
showq / joblist             # cluster-wide queue overviews
pestat                      # per-node CPU/memory load across the cluster






arccq does not exist



Some docs mention an arccq command as an alternative to squeue. It isn’t installed on MedicineBow — use squeue, showuserjobs, or joblist instead.




7.1.4 Cancelling
scancel 123456              # cancel one job
scancel --me                # cancel ALL my jobs (careful)
scancel --me --state=PENDING   # cancel only my still-waiting jobs
scancel 123456_7            # cancel one element of a job array (@sec-arrays)


7.1.5 A monitoring routine
For a job you care about:

sbatch submit.sh → note the job ID.
squeue --me → is it PD or R? If PD for a while, showjobreasons <id>.
Running → tail -f slurm-<id>.out.
Done → seff <id> to right-size the next one.

title: 7  Monitoring, arrays, and interactive jobs
text:
7.2 Job arrays

7.2.1 The problem it solves
You have 500 parameter combinations to sweep, or 500 raster tiles / watersheds / weather-days to process. A bash loop runs them serially in one job, so one crash near the end wastes everything. Copy-pasting 500 submit scripts is no better. An array job is one script, submitted once, that Slurm turns into 500 independent tasks it can run in parallel and backfill wherever there’s room.


7.2.2 The mechanics
Add --array and use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to pick which piece of work this task does:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=cowy-firesurro
#SBATCH --job-name=sweep
#SBATCH --array=1-500                 # 500 tasks, indices 1..500
#SBATCH --qos=fast                    # short independent tasks → high-priority QOS
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00               # per task
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=logs/sweep-%A_%a.out # %A = array job id, %a = task index

module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 python/3.12.0

# Use the task index to select this task's work:
python run_case.py --case-id ${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}
Submit once:
mkdir -p logs
sbatch submit_array.sh        # creates 500 tasks: 12345_1, 12345_2, ... 12345_500
Each task is scheduled independently. Because they’re small and short, they backfill well (Section 6.3) and the whole sweep finishes faster than running them in series.


7.2.3 Driving work from the index
The index is just a number; you map it to real work. Common patterns:
Line N of a parameter file:
PARAM=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" params.txt)
python run.py $PARAM
The Nth input file:
FILES=(/project/cowy-firesurro/data/tiles/*.tif)
THIS=${FILES[$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID]}      # note: arrays are 0-indexed in bash
python process.py "$THIS"
(If you index files from a bash array, start --array=0; if you use sed -n Np, start --array=1. Off-by-one here is the classic array bug.)


7.2.4 Throttling
Cap how many tasks run simultaneously with %:
#SBATCH --array=1-500%20        # at most 20 tasks running at a time
This keeps you under your account’s core cap (and protects your fair-share, Section 6.3) while still processing all 500. A modest % limit is often faster overall, because you stop competing with yourself and stay backfill-friendly.


7.2.5 Managing an array
squeue --me                     # shows pending tasks collapsed, e.g. 12345_[6-500]
scancel 12345                   # cancel the whole array
scancel 12345_7                 # cancel just task 7
sacct -j 12345                  # per-task outcomes after the fact
To find which tasks failed (so you can rerun only those):
sacct -j 12345 --format=JobID,State,ExitCode -n | grep -v COMPLETED
then resubmit just those indices: sbatch --array=17,43,88 submit_array.sh.






Arrays vs. MPI jobs



An array is for independent tasks that don’t communicate: sweeps, ensembles, per-file pipelines. If your tasks must talk to each other — a single domain-decomposed simulation — use an MPI job instead (Section 7.4).


Arrays are also the natural unit for ensembles — fire-weather members, hydrologic scenarios, Monte-Carlo draws — one array task per member, each writing to its own output, collected afterward.

title: 7  Monitoring, arrays, and interactive jobs
text:
7.3 Interactive sessions and GPU jobs

7.3.1 Interactive sessions with salloc
For hands-on work — debugging a crash, exploring a dataset, building a model interactively — request an interactive allocation:
salloc --account=cowy-firesurro --qos=interactive \
       --time=02:00:00 --cpus-per-task=4 --mem=16G
salloc requires at least --account and --time. It grants a shell on a compute node, where you can run heavy work off the login node. The interactive QOS starts in ~10–30 seconds (Section 6.2) with an 8-hour ceiling.






Launch salloc from inside tmux



An interactive session lives in your shell. If your laptop sleeps or WiFi drops, the shell dies and the session ends. Start tmux on the login node first, then salloc inside it (Section 2.6). You can then detach, close the laptop, and reattach later with the session intact, as long as it’s within your --time.


When you’re done, exit the shell to release the allocation and free the cores for others.

7.3.1.1 Interactive apps in the portal
The web portal (Section 1.3) offers graphical interactive apps — a full XFCE desktop, RStudio, and Jupyter — that launch as scheduled jobs behind the scenes. These handle interactive and GPU notebook work without manual salloc and port-forwarding.



7.3.2 GPU jobs
Request GPUs with --gres=gpu:<count> and target a GPU partition:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=cowy-firesurro
#SBATCH --partition=mb-l40s          # or mb-h100, mb-a30, ...
#SBATCH --qos=normal
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                 # one GPU on the node
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8            # CPUs to feed the GPU
#SBATCH --mem=64G
#SBATCH --time=08:00:00

module purge
module load gcc/13.2.0 cuda-toolkit/12.6.1   # CUDA needs gcc 13.2, see below
nvidia-smi                                    # confirm the GPU is visible
python train.py
To request a specific GPU type you can also use the typed form, e.g. --gres=gpu:h100:2 for two H100s on one node.

Develop on A30s, not H100s



H100 nodes are the most contended resource on the machine — waits of several hours are normal when they’re busy (Section 6.2). Do fast-iteration development on A30s, usually available in minutes, and submit to mb-h100 only for a real training run that needs it. Check gpuavail and showpartitions before choosing.








GPU compiler requirement



cuda-toolkit is built only against gcc/13.2.0, even though gcc/13.2.0 prints a deprecation warning pointing to gcc/14.2.0. For GPU/CUDA work, load gcc/13.2.0 and ignore the warning (Section 4.1). Inside containers, add --nv to expose the GPU (Section 4.2).




7.3.2.2 Checking GPU availability and usage
gpuavail                    # ARCC helper: free GPUs by type, right now
slurm_gpustat               # cluster-wide GPU utilization
sinfo -p mb-h100 -o "%P %t %G %D"   # H100 node states this second
nvidia-smi                  # inside a GPU job: is my code actually using the GPU?
nvtop                       # inside a GPU job: live GPU usage, like htop for GPUs
If nvidia-smi shows 0% utilization while your job runs, your code isn’t actually on the GPU. Verify early.

text:
7.4 The parallelism ladder

7.4.1 Climb only as high as you need
MPI and GPUs sound like “real HPC,” but the right answer is usually lower on the ladder and simpler. Match the rung to the shape of your problem.






flowchart LR
    A["Serial<br/>1 core"] --> B["Job array<br/>many independent runs"]
    B --> C["Multicore<br/>threads, 1 node"]
    C --> D["MPI<br/>1 program, many nodes"]
    D --> E["GPU<br/>ML / PINNs"]
    style B stroke-width:3px,stroke:#4a2c82




Figure 7.2: The parallelism ladder. Climb only as high as the problem needs; most work is solved at the job-array rung (highlighted).






7.4.1.1 Rung 1 — Serial
One core, one task. Fine for small jobs, and the right baseline: get it correct on one core first. If a serial job is fast enough, you’re done — don’t parallelize unnecessarily.
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1


7.4.1.2 Rung 2 — Job array (many independent serial runs)
If you need to run the same thing many times over different inputs — a parameter sweep, an ensemble, per-file processing — this is almost always the answer. Low complexity, and it backfills well (Section 7.2).
#SBATCH --array=1-500%20
python run.py --id ${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}


7.4.1.3 Rung 3 — Multicore (one program, many threads, one node)
If a single run is too slow and your code is multithreaded (OpenMP, or numpy/xarray/PyTorch using many cores), give it more cores on one node:
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
./my_threaded_program
Only ask for as many cores as your code actually scales to — check with seff afterward (Section 5.3). Doubling cores rarely doubles speed.


7.4.1.4 Rung 4 — MPI (one program across many nodes)
When a single problem is too big for one node — a domain-decomposed simulation like WRF, where pieces must exchange data every step — you need MPI: one program, many processes across many nodes, communicating.
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks=384                 # e.g. 96 tasks/node × 4 nodes
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1

module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 openmpi/5.0.10
srun ./my_mpi_simulation             # srun launches the MPI ranks
Use srun (not mpirun) to launch — it’s integrated with Slurm and gets the task layout right automatically. MPI is a step up in complexity; use it only when a problem won’t fit on one node. For long MPI runs, prefer non-investor and checkpoint (Section 8.1).


7.4.1.5 Rung 5 — GPU
For workloads built for GPUs — deep learning, PINNs, some CFD/linear algebra — a GPU can beat dozens of CPU cores, but only if your code actually targets the GPU (Section 7.3.2); a CPU program gains nothing from a GPU node except a longer queue. Develop on mb-a30, scale up to mb-h100 for real training (Section 6.2).
#SBATCH --partition=mb-a30
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
module load gcc/13.2.0 cuda-toolkit/12.6.1
python train.py



7.4.2 Choosing a rung







Your situation
Rung




It’s already fast enough
Serial


“Run this many times over different inputs”
Job array (start here)


One run is slow; code uses threads
Multicore


One problem too big for a single node; parts must communicate
MPI


Code is written for GPUs (ML/PINN)
GPU



You can combine rungs — e.g. an array of multicore jobs (a sweep where each run uses 8 cores), which covers a large fraction of real research computing. Start as low as you can; climb only when you need to.

text:
8.1 Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing
How long jobs survive preemption and walltime limits, and how to diagnose jobs that fail.

title: 8  Preemption, checkpointing, and failures
text:
8.1.1 The condo model
Much of MedicineBow’s hardware was bought by individual research groups, departments, or PIs using their own grant or startup funds. Those buyers are the investors, and the nodes they paid for make up the inv-* partitions, where they get top priority (QOS 110). Everyone else can backfill onto idle investor nodes — free capacity most of the time, with one condition.






An investor can reclaim a node and requeue your job



If you land on investor hardware and the owner submits work, your job is preempted — Slurm kills it and, by default here, requeues it: it returns to the pending queue and starts over from the beginning when resources free up. Any progress not written to disk is lost. This can happen minutes into a job or days in.




8.1.2 Two ways to protect a long run
1. Run where you can’t be preempted. Submit long production jobs to the non-preemptible pool:
#SBATCH --partition=non-investor        # 110 CPU nodes, not reclaimable
# or non-investor-gpu for GPU work
This is the right home for anything long that you haven’t checkpointed. (The --constraint=non-investor some docs mention does not work — it’s a partition, not a constraint. See Section 6.1.)
2. Checkpoint, so preemption is cheap. If you run on borrowable hardware (or list several partitions for faster starts), save state periodically so a requeue is survivable.


8.1.3 Checkpointing
A checkpoint is a periodic save of enough state to resume rather than restart. It protects against preemption, node failures, and hitting your walltime limit. Any job measured in days should checkpoint.
The pattern:

Every so often (every N iterations, or every ~30–60 min of wall time), write current state to a checkpoint file in /gscratch or /project — not /lscratch, which is wiped when the job ends (Section 3.1).
On startup, check for a checkpoint and resume from it if present, otherwise start fresh.
Write checkpoints atomically (write to a temp file, then rename) so a crash mid-write can’t corrupt your only checkpoint. Keep the last one or two.

Many scientific codes have this built in — WRF has restart files, PyTorch has torch.save/load for model+optimizer state, PETSc and Sundials have checkpoint hooks. Turn these on and set the interval to your risk tolerance.
Auto-resubmit on requeue. Combine checkpointing with a self-resubmitting job so a preempted or timed-out job resumes automatically:
#SBATCH --requeue                          # allow this job to be requeued
#SBATCH --open-mode=append                 # don't clobber the log on requeue
#SBATCH --signal=B:USR1@120                # send USR1 120s before the walltime kill

# resume from checkpoint if one exists
if [ -f state.ckpt ]; then
    ./simulate --restart state.ckpt
else
    ./simulate --fresh
fi
The --signal line asks Slurm to warn your script 120 seconds before the walltime kill; trap that signal to flush a final checkpoint.


8.1.4 Requeue behavior worth knowing

A requeued job keeps its job ID but starts its command from the beginning — Slurm doesn’t magically resume your program; your checkpoint does.
--open-mode=append stops the requeued run from overwriting the previous log.
Check whether a job was requeued with sacct -j <id> --format=JobID,State,Start,End — you’ll see multiple rows.







Checkpoint jobs that run longer than a few hours



Short jobs (minutes to an hour or two) can just be rerun if something goes wrong. Any multi-hour or multi-day job should checkpoint, and any long production run should also prefer non-investor. A non-preemptible partition plus checkpoints is what lets big simulations finish reliably on a shared machine.

title: 8  Preemption, checkpointing, and failures
text:
8.2 When jobs fail

8.2.1 Step one: what state did it end in?
sacct -j 123456 --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,MaxRSS,ReqMem,DerivedExitCode
The State column is your first clue:








State
Meaning
Usual fix




COMPLETED
exit code 0
none (but check the output is correct)


OUT_OF_MEMORY
killed by the OOM killer
raise --mem (see below)


TIMEOUT
hit the --time limit
raise --time, or checkpoint (Section 8.1.3)


FAILED
your program exited non-zero
read the .out/.err file — it’s your bug


NODE_FAIL
the hardware died
resubmit; checkpoint so it’s cheap


PREEMPTED / REQUEUED
investor reclaimed the node
Section 8.1


CANCELLED
someone ran scancel (maybe you)
—





8.2.2 Out of memory
A job that exceeds its memory reservation is killed by the Linux OOM killer — you’ll see OUT_OF_MEMORY in sacct, and often a truncated or empty output file.
sacct -j 123456 --format=JobID,State,MaxRSS,ReqMem
# MaxRSS is peak memory actually used; compare to ReqMem
If MaxRSS is near or above ReqMem, raise --mem and resubmit. Then use seff (Section 7.1) on the successful run to right-size going forward. Note the 10 GB/core default on mb (Section 5.3) — sometimes you already had enough memory and something else was wrong.


8.2.3 Timeout
TIMEOUT means your job was still running when the clock ran out and Slurm killed it. Options, in order of preference:

Checkpoint so the next run resumes instead of restarting (Section 8.1.3). This is the durable fix for genuinely long work.
Raise --time — but staying under your QOS ceiling (normal = 3 d, long = 7 d), and knowing a longer request may wait longer to start (Section 6.2).
Make the job finish faster — more cores if it scales, or a smaller problem per job (an array, Section 7.2).



8.2.4 Your program crashed (FAILED)
FAILED with a non-zero exit code is usually your code, not the cluster. Read the output:
cat slurm-123456.out          # stdout+stderr (or separate --error file)
Common cluster-specific culprits:

Module not loaded in the script. Interactive worked, batch didn’t — because you loaded modules on the login node but not inside the submit script. Put module load in the script (Section 5.2).
Wrong paths. A relative path that existed where you ran sbatch but not where the job ran. Use absolute paths or $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR.
conda env not activated in the script (Section 4.2).
Wrote to /lscratch and it vanished — that’s node-local and wiped at job end (Section 3.1).



8.2.5 Node failure and preemption
NODE_FAIL (hardware died) and PREEMPTED/REQUEUED (investor reclaimed the node, Section 8.1) are not your bug. The response is the same: checkpoint so a restart is cheap, run long jobs on non-investor, and add --requeue so they come back automatically. If node failures recur on the same node, report it to arcc-help@uwyo.edu with the job ID.


8.2.6 A debugging loop

sacct -j <id> ... → get the State, narrowing it to one of the four families above.
Resource-related (OOM/timeout) → adjust --mem/--time, resubmit.
FAILED → read slurm-<id>.out, fix the code/env, and reproduce it fast in a debug-QOS job (near-instant start, Section 6.2) rather than waiting in a long queue each iteration.
Once it works, seff <id> → right-size → promote to the real partition/QOS.

Use the debug partition as your fast edit-run-debug loop, and graduate to big queues only once the job is known-good.

title: 9  Reference
text:
9.2 Troubleshooting
A symptom-first index to the rest of the book.

9.2.1 Login and access
“Permission denied (publickey)” when I ssh — it worked before. Your SSH key almost certainly expired (they last one year). Regenerate it in the portal’s SSH Key Manager, unzip into ~/.ssh, chmod 0600 -R ~/.ssh (Section 1.3).
“Permission denied” on a brand-new setup. Check permissions: chmod 0600 -R ~/.ssh, and make sure you unzipped the key into ~/.ssh. Confirm you’re using medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu, not the dead southpass name.
I can’t get an account at all. Only a PI can request it, in writing, against a project. You cannot self-register (Section 1.2).
Globus won’t let me add the collection. If you’re an external collaborator on an ARCC-Only account, you can’t use Globus. You need a UW-side guest collection (Section 3.2).


9.2.2 Jobs won’t submit
sbatch: error: ... You have to specify an account. Add --account=cowy-firesurro (Section 5.2).
Job violates accounting/QOS policy (...) at submit time. Your request exceeds a QOS limit (every QOS is DenyOnLimit). Usually --time exceeds the QOS ceiling — e.g. 5 days under normal (max 3 d). Lower --time or switch QOS (Section 6.1). Check ceilings with sqos and showuserlimits.
Invalid qos specification. Your account can’t use that QOS. Yours are debug, fast, interactive, long, normal (sacctmgr -n show assoc user=$USER format=qos).


9.2.3 Jobs won’t start
Stuck in PENDING with reason Priority. The machine is just busy and you’re in line. Either wait, or pick a higher-priority (shorter) QOS — QOS dominates priority here (Section 6.3). Small/short jobs backfill sooner.
Stuck with reason Resources. You asked for a lot (many cores, much memory, a scarce GPU). Right-size (Section 5.3), or accept the wait. showjobreasons <id> explains in plain language.
GPU job pending for hours. H100/L40S are heavily contended (Section 6.2). Develop on mb-a30 instead, and check gpuavail/showpartitions for what’s actually free before submitting.
Pending with QOSMax... or AssocGrpCpuLimit. You (or your account) hit a cap — e.g. too many cores in flight at once. Wait for your other jobs to finish, or throttle an array with % (Section 7.2).


9.2.4 Jobs fail
OUT_OF_MEMORY. Raise --mem. Compare MaxRSS to ReqMem in sacct (Section 8.2). Watch the 10 GB/core default trap (Section 5.3).
TIMEOUT. Job outran --time. Checkpoint (Section 8.1.3), raise --time within the QOS ceiling, or split the work into an array.
FAILED, worked interactively but not in batch. You loaded modules / activated conda on the login node but not inside the submit script. Put them in the script (Section 5.2, Section 4.2).
Output file references files that “don’t exist.” Relative paths from the wrong directory, or you wrote to /lscratch (wiped at job end). Use absolute paths or $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR; copy /lscratch output out before the job ends (Section 3.1).
PREEMPTED / REQUEUED on a long job. You were on investor hardware and got reclaimed. Move to --partition=non-investor and checkpoint (Section 8.1).


9.2.5 Software
“That module doesn’t exist” but I’m sure it does. module avail only shows what’s reachable now. Use module spider <name> — you probably need to load a compiler first (Section 4.1).
CUDA won’t build / link. Load gcc/13.2.0 (not 14) — cuda-toolkit is built against 13.2 despite its deprecation warning (Section 4.1).
Home directory full, everything breaking. Conda in /home. Move envs to /project/<proj>/software via ~/.condarc, and clean up (Section 4.2). Check with du -sh ~/* | sort -h.
GPU job runs but is slow / nvidia-smi shows 0%. Your code isn’t actually on the GPU. Verify the framework sees CUDA; in a container, you need --nv (Section 7.3.2).


9.2.6 Still stuck?
Email arcc-help@uwyo.edu with your job ID, the submit script, and the error. Or bring it to office hours, Tuesdays 11am–1pm on Zoom. Include what you already tried — it gets you a faster answer.

9.3 Glossary
Plain-language definitions of the terms this book uses.

Account (Slurm)

The project that a job is charged to (e.g. cowy-firesurro). Required on every job via --account. Not your username. See Section 5.2.

ARCC

Advanced Research Computing Center — the UW group that runs MedicineBow.

ASCEND / ARID

The NSF Regional Innovation Engine (ASCEND) and its wildfire-resilience program (ARID) that many readers of this book work under. See the preface.

Backfill

Slurm slotting a small, short job into a gap in the schedule without delaying higher-priority jobs. Why short jobs start fast. See Section 6.3.

Batch job

A job submitted as a script with sbatch that runs unattended when scheduled. The normal way to run work. See Section 5.2.

Checkpoint

A periodic save of a job’s state so it can resume instead of restart after a preemption, timeout, or crash. Essential for long jobs. See Section 8.1.3.

Compute node

A machine where computation actually runs, allocated to you by Slurm. Distinct from a login node. See Section 1.1.

Condo model

The funding model where research groups buy nodes (inv-*) and others borrow them when idle, subject to reclaim/preemption. See Section 8.1.

Core-hour

One CPU core used for one hour — the unit your allocation is measured in. Reserving 8 cores for 1 hour costs 8 core-hours whether or not you use them.

DenyOnLimit

A QOS flag meaning an over-limit request is rejected at submit time, not silently queued. See Section 6.1.

Fair-share

A priority factor reflecting your account’s recent usage relative to its share; heavy recent use temporarily lowers your priority. See Section 6.3.

GRES (Generic RESource)

How you request GPUs: --gres=gpu:1 or --gres=gpu:h100:2. See Section 7.3.2.

Investor / inv-*

A research group, department, or PI that bought cluster nodes with their own funds. Their inv-* partitions give them top priority; jobs others backfill there can be preempted. See Section 8.1.

Job array

One script run many times with a varying index ($SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID), for parameter sweeps and ensembles. Max 10,000 tasks. See Section 7.2.

Lmod / module

The system that loads specific software versions into your shell on demand. Hierarchical: many modules are hidden until you load a compiler. Use module spider. See Section 4.1.

Login node

The shared front-end machine (mblog1, mblog2) you land on when you connect. For editing and submitting — not for computing. See Section 1.1.

MedicineBow

UW/ARCC’s current flagship HPC cluster. The subject of this book.

MPI

Message Passing Interface — the standard for a single parallel program spanning many cores or nodes that communicate. Launched with srun. Contrast with job arrays. See Section 7.4.

OnDemand (Open OnDemand)

The web portal at medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu — file browser, terminal, and interactive apps. See Section 1.3.

OOM (Out Of Memory)

When a job exceeds its memory reservation and is killed. Fix by raising --mem. See Section 8.2.

Partition

A named pool of nodes with particular hardware (mb, mb-h100, teton, non-investor, …). Chosen with --partition. See Section 6.1.

Preemption

An investor reclaiming a borrowed node, causing your job to be killed and (here) requeued. See Section 8.1.

Priority

The score that orders pending jobs. On MedicineBow it’s dominated by QOS (weight 200). See Section 6.3.

QOS (Quality of Service)

The service tier that sets your max walltime, resource cap, and priority (debug, fast, normal, long, …). See Section 6.1.

Requeue

Putting a killed (preempted/failed) job back in the pending queue to start over. Pair with checkpointing. See Section 8.1.

Scratch (/gscratch, $SCRATCH)

Fast, large, temporary storage purged after 90 days of inactivity. Not backed up. See Section 3.1.

seff

A command showing a finished job’s CPU and memory efficiency — use it to right-size. See Section 7.1.

Slurm

The scheduler that manages all jobs on the cluster. See Section 5.1.

Snapshot

A point-in-time copy of a filesystem, on the same array as the live data. Protects against accidental deletion, not hardware loss. Not a backup. See Section 3.1.

Walltime

Real elapsed clock time a job is allowed (--time). The job is killed at the limit. See Section 5.3.
